title: Follow a request all the way through
summary: A practical way to see where a service creates extra work.
paragraphs: Choose a request which matters to somebody using the service. Follow it from the point where the need arose to the point where the person received a useful response. Keep the person’s purpose in view. Closing a case on a system may be only one event in their attempt to get something done.

Ask the staff involved to reconstruct the work from the records they actually use. Include handovers, waiting, repeated contacts, checks, rework, and effort by the person outside the organisation. A diagram is useful if it allows people to point to a specific difficulty and explain how it arose.

Several explanations may fit the same event. A repeated telephone call could arise from unclear information, a delayed decision, an inaccessible form, or a change in the person’s circumstances. Collect enough evidence to distinguish them before choosing a response. Labelling all repeat contact as failure demand conceals work which may be necessary.

Bring the people responsible for the different stages together around this account. Ask which changes are within their authority, which rules constrain them, and which decisions need a different owner. Start with a change small enough to observe: a clearer message, a different handover, or a decision taken closer to the work.

Review the effect on the person’s experience, staff effort, and the eventual outcome. A faster transaction which creates another contact elsewhere has moved the work. Keep following the request until you can see whether the whole service has improved.

title: Assurance that helps people decide
summary: Make reporting useful to the people who must act.
paragraphs: Start with a consequential decision. Who makes it, when, and what could change their judgement? This gives a report a purpose. A large set of measures can describe activity while leaving the decision-maker unable to tell whether action is needed.

For each measure, ask what observation would cause somebody to intervene. Check whether that person has the authority and resources to do so. Where a measure has no plausible connection to action, establish whether it serves a separate obligation, such as statutory reporting, before removing it.

People doing the work often know about a difficulty before it appears in the aggregate numbers. Give that knowledge a route into the decision. A short account of an awkward case may reveal a conflict between targets, eligibility rules, and people’s actual circumstances.

Agree how uncertainty and disagreement will be reported. A red rating with an honest account of what is unknown can be more useful than a green rating maintained by narrowing the definition. The response from senior leaders will determine whether people continue to bring inconvenient evidence.

Review the reporting arrangement itself after a decision. Did the information arrive in time? Did it identify the choices and consequences? Did anyone affected have a meaningful opportunity to challenge the account? Use the answers to simplify and improve assurance.

title: Where is the work going?
summary: Understand demand, effort, and capacity before deciding what to cut.
paragraphs: A budget identifies what an organisation spends. It rarely explains adequately what its people spend their time doing, why that work arrives, or which activities make a useful difference. Resource optimisation begins by bringing those accounts together.

Work with teams to identify recurring activities and the demand behind them. Use a manageable level of detail. The purpose is to understand the pattern of effort and the constraints on useful work, rather than create an elaborate timesheet for every movement.

Distinguish work which creates value, work which supports it, work required by a legitimate obligation, and work generated by avoidable failure or friction. These categories require judgement. Something which looks unnecessary from one position may protect someone elsewhere.

Test an opportunity against its wider consequences. Stopping a check could release time and increase risk. Moving a task to another team could reduce one budget while raising total effort. Bringing a decision closer to the service could reduce delay while requiring better access to advice.

Give each proposed change an owner, an evidence base, and a way to observe the result. Report released capacity separately from cashable savings. Time becomes a budget saving only when a concrete and sustainable financial change follows.

title: A partnership needs decisions it can make
summary: Start with authority and obligations when cross-boundary work stalls.
paragraphs: When a partnership repeatedly returns to the same unresolved issue, inspect the decision it is trying to make. The people in the room may agree on the desired outcome while lacking authority to commit their organisations, budgets, or colleagues.

Draw a simple account of the decision: whose agreement is required, who can stop it, who will carry the work, and who bears the consequences. Include people affected by the decision who have no seat at the table. An invitation to comment is different from influence over the choice.

Ask each organisation to state the obligations it cannot set aside. These may include financial duties, professional standards, political commitments, contracts, or accountability to a community. Treat these as material for design. Pretending that shared purpose has removed them produces agreements which unravel outside the meeting.

Separate a joint decision from coordinated decisions. Sometimes the feasible arrangement is for several organisations to make distinct commitments, connected by a shared review and a clear escalation route. Make those commitments specific enough that someone can tell whether they happened.

Choose the next review around the work. Examine what changed, which promises held, and which new difficulties appeared. The partnership becomes more capable when its members can revise their arrangements in the light of experience.

title: Commission the conditions for useful work
summary: Examine what the funding and contract make possible.
paragraphs: A commissioned service operates within conditions set by funding, contract terms, performance expectations, information, and the relationships between commissioners, providers, and the people receiving support. These conditions can matter as much as the service specification.

Take one outcome you want to improve. Ask what providers and practitioners need to be able to do differently. Do they need time to build trust, discretion to adapt support, cooperation with another service, or permission to question an assumption?

Compare that need with the actual arrangement. A short funding period may undermine continuity. A narrow output target may discourage useful work outside the measured activity. A payment rule may shift risk to an organisation which has little capacity to carry it.

There are legitimate reasons for controls, specifications, and public accountability. Work out what each protects and whether the same protection can be achieved through a more useful arrangement. Involve finance, procurement, assurance, providers, and people using support early enough for their knowledge to affect the design.

Agree how the parties will learn together and what would justify a change to the contract or service. Record the decisions, their rationale, and the boundaries of discretion. Adaptation requires accountability which can describe why a different response became necessary.

title: Build capability through a live problem
summary: Design development around work participants must actually do.
paragraphs: Select a piece of work which participants have some ability to influence. It should be consequential enough to sustain attention and bounded enough to permit action during the programme. A hypothetical case can introduce a method; it cannot establish whether participants can use it in their own setting.

Agree the relationship between learning and delivery. Sponsors need to know what time, access, and decision authority participants require. Participants need room to discover that the original brief was incomplete or that the proposed solution was wrong.

Teach a method when it helps participants make a better observation, distinction, or decision. Ask them to explain what they used, what it allowed them to see, and what it left out. Competence includes recognising when a familiar method is a poor fit.

Build short cycles of application and review between sessions. Keep evidence of the work, including mistakes and changes of mind. Peer discussion becomes more useful when people bring a real choice and its consequences rather than an account designed to demonstrate progress.

At the end, review what participants can now do, the changes their work produced, and the conditions needed to sustain both. A certificate records completion. Continued capability depends on practice, support, and an organisation willing to use what people have learned.
